newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada's Goodale says to proceed with CWB bill.
newsitem.headline: Canada's Goodale says to proceed with CWB bill.

text.p: Ralph Goodale, Canada's minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board (CWB), said on Wednesday he expected to quickly reintroduce legislation on making changes to the operation of the CWB.

Among the amendments to the CWB Act, which failed to clear Parliament before the snap elections called in April by Prime Minister Jean Chretien, is one that would allow the CWB export monopoly to make cash, or spot, grain purchases.
Price pooling, or one price for all farmers, had been a founding principle of the CWB when it was formed in 1935.
"My expectation is that we will pick up that legislation as quickly as possible and move forward with it," Goodale said of the CWB Act amendments.

"Obviously the time frame is now somewhat different than would have been the case had the legislation been adopted in the spring, so there will need to be a variety of technical adjustments, but the fundamental principles certainly remain in place."
But there seemed little likelihood for now of an end to the monopoly the CWB maintains over barley and wheat exports, with Goodale maintaining responsibility for the CWB.

Goodale supervised a referendum on whether the monopoly should end. The answer was no, but he drew fire from the market-oriented Reform Party, dominant in the West, for not allowing the possibility of farmers selling some grain on the free market while continuing to maintain the CWB.
Goodale, the only Liberal member of Parliament left in Saskatchewan, moved from agriculture to natural resources in a cabinet shuffle on Wednesday but maintained responsibility for the CWB.
"I think Goodale is bad for the Wheat Board and western producers. I think it would be best for him to be out of there entirely," Reform leader Preston Manning told a news conference.
"There's a need for reform at the Wheat Board and it's not going to happen as long as Mr. Goodale's responsible for it."
Goodale said that when campaigning last month he did not find the Wheat Board to be a burning issue.

"It was generally me that raised it, asking farmers what their opinion was, and generally the comment would come back that producers would not want to see as a general principle the Canadian Wheat Board weakened or impaired," he said.
"But they did want more democracy, they wanted more accountability, they wanted more flexibility and responsiveness."
That essentially was what the government's CWB legislation would implement, he said.

Ontario fruit and vegetable farmer Lyle Vanclief replaced him at agriculture but said it would be more Goodale's responsibility to deal with delays in getting grain to market, such as those this past winter.
Goodale said there was also a role on that issue for the transport and agriculture ministers.
He added there were frequent precedents in the past for responsibility for the CWB to be assigned to a western Canadian minister.
